summary: Dexmedetomidine is an IV alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used for sedation of initially intubated, mechanically ventilated adults in the ICU and for procedural sedation of non-intubated adults. Typical dosing is a 1 mcg/kg loading infusion over 10 minutes followed by 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h (ICU) titrated to effect; administration should not exceed 24 hours. Bradycardia, hypotension and sinus arrest are the principal hazards, with withdrawal and tolerance after prolonged use.
indications: Sedation of initially intubated and mechanically ventilated adult patients during treatment in an intensive care setting (continuous infusion not to exceed 24 hours)
Sedation of non-intubated adult patients prior to and/or during surgical and other procedures (procedural sedation)

dosage.d: 1 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes (loading dose may not be needed when converting from another sedative)
dosage.n: Consider dose reduction in patients >65 years or hepatic impairment

dosage.d: 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h, titrated to desired level of sedation
dosage.t: Continuous infusion, not to exceed 24 hours
dosage.n: Reduce for age >65 or hepatic impairment

dosage.d: 1 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes (0.5 mcg/kg over 10 min for less invasive procedures e.g. ophthalmic, and for patients >65 years)
dosage.n: Awake fiberoptic intubation: 1 mcg/kg over 10 minutes

dosage.d: Initiate at 0.6 mcg/kg/h, titrate 0.2-1 mcg/kg/h to effect
dosage.n: Awake fiberoptic intubation: 0.7 mcg/kg/h until endotracheal tube secured

admin: Administer only by personnel skilled in managing patients in the ICU or operating room setting, using a controlled infusion device
Dexmedetomidine Injection (100 mcg/mL) MUST be diluted to 4 mcg/mL with 0.9% sodium chloride before use; the 5% dextrose ready-to-use bags (4 mcg/mL) need no further dilution
Continuously monitor blood pressure, heart rate and oxygenation during and after administration
Administration duration should not exceed 24 hours
Avoid rapid IV or bolus administration (associated with bradycardia and sinus arrest); titrate to clinical effect

It is not necessary to discontinue before extubation; use synthetic or coated natural-rubber administration components (drug absorbs into some natural rubber); do not co-administer with blood/plasma or with amphotericin B or diazepam
moa: Dexmedetomidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist. Stimulation of central (locus coeruleus) alpha-2 receptors reduces sympathetic outflow and norepinephrine release, producing sedation, anxiolysis and analgesia without significant respiratory depression. The reduced sympathetic tone also accounts for the characteristic dose-related hypotension and bradycardia.

relative: Advanced heart block (2nd/3rd degree) without pacemaker
monitor: Concomitant vasodilators or negative chronotropic agents
Diabetes mellitus or chronic hypertension (more pronounced hemodynamic effects)

preg: Published data over decades of IV use have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage, though most exposures occurred after the first trimester (often at cesarean delivery, without adverse effect on maternal outcomes or infant Apgar scores). Dexmedetomidine crosses the placenta; animal studies showed fetal/developmental toxicity at doses near or above the human dose.
lact: Dexmedetomidine is present in human milk. Because of its short half-life, advising the patient to discard milk and not breastfeed during treatment and for the period after the last dose minimizes infant exposure. Monitor breastfed infants for irritability or sedation.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is provided in the labeling. Use with general caution and monitor hemodynamics.
hepatic: Clearance decreases with increasing severity of hepatic impairment; consider a dose reduction in patients with impaired hepatic function.

major: Anesthetics, sedatives, hypnotics, opioids (sevoflurane, isoflurane, propofol, alfentanil, midazolam) - enhanced sedative/respiratory depressant effect; reduce dose of dexmedetomidine or the co-administered agent
moderate: Vasodilators and negative chronotropic agents - additive hypotension/bradycardia
minor: Neuromuscular blockers (e.g., rocuronium) - no clinically meaningful change in blockade observed
interactions.alcohol: Additive CNS and respiratory depression; relevant if alcohol present.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause transient hypertension during loading, then hypotension/bradycardia; monitor ECG and blood pressure.

serious: Withdrawal (nausea, vomiting, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension) after >24 h use
ARDS / respiratory failure with infusions >24 hours
emergency: Sinus arrest or severe bradycardia with hemodynamic compromise

monitoring: Continuous blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation during infusion and after discontinuation
ECG for bradyarrhythmias, AV block or sinus arrest
Urine output and serum sodium/osmolality if diabetes insipidus is suspected, especially with prolonged use
Body temperature; signs of withdrawal/tachyphylaxis with use beyond 24 hours
counsel: This medicine is given as an IV drip in a monitored setting to keep you calm and sedated
Your blood pressure, heart rate and breathing will be watched continuously
You may feel drowsy but can still be roused when spoken to or stimulated, which is normal
Tell the care team about heart rhythm problems, low blood pressure, or all other medicines you take
After the infusion you may feel temporarily restless or have a fast heartbeat, which staff will manage
pk: Sedation within minutes of loading infusion
Effect at end of 10-minute loading infusion
Effect dissipates within ~1-2 hours after stopping
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); diluted solution up to 4 h room temp or 24 h at 2-8 C
pearls: Provides cooperative sedation with minimal respiratory depression - patients remain arousable
Avoid rapid IV/bolus dosing: it triggers bradycardia and sinus arrest
Labeled not to exceed 24 hours; beyond this expect tolerance, tachyphylaxis and more adverse events
Atropine or glycopyrrolate treats most dexmedetomidine-induced bradycardia
Transient hypertension during the loading dose reflects peripheral vasoconstriction; consider slowing the load
missed: Administered by a clinician as a titrated IV infusion; not self-dosed. The care team adjusts or stops the infusion to clinical effect; avoid abrupt discontinuation after prolonged (>24 h) use because of withdrawal.
overdose: Overdose may cause first-degree AV block, second-degree heart block, bradycardia and hypotension; an inadvertent undiluted loading bolus has caused cardiac arrest (successfully resuscitated). Management is supportive: stop the infusion, support hemodynamics with IV fluids, leg elevation, anticholinergics (atropine/glycopyrrolate) and pressors as needed; the heart block observed in volunteers resolved spontaneously.
